title: Nearby Places Search
prompt: Design a service that shows people restaurants, shops and other places near where they are standing, and lets business owners keep their listings up to date.

clarify.q: What search radius do users pick, and is there a maximum?
clarify.why: The radius decides the cell size of the geo index. A 500 m walk and a 20 km drive need very different precision, and an unbounded radius would scan whole regions.

clarify.q: How many places are listed, and how many searches per day?
clarify.why: 200 M places at ~32 B per index entry is about 6 GB, which fits in memory on one machine. That single fact decides whether we shard the index or just replicate it.

clarify.q: How quickly must a new or edited listing appear in search?
clarify.why: If minutes are fine, we can rebuild or update the index asynchronously from the database. Instant visibility would force synchronous index writes on every edit.

clarify.q: How are results ordered: pure distance, or a mix of distance, rating and relevance?
clarify.why: Pure distance can stop early at the nearest cells. Blended ranking must fetch a larger candidate set before sorting, which changes the per-query cost.

clarify.q: Do we filter by category, price or 'open now'?
clarify.why: Filters shrink results after the geo lookup. Very common filters (category) may deserve their own index per category so dense cities do not scan thousands of irrelevant places.

clarify.q: Are moving things (food trucks, drivers) in scope?
clarify.why: Moving objects make the index write-heavy, which is a different design. Fixed businesses change rarely, so the index can be built for reads.

functional: Given a location and a radius (up to 20 km), return nearby places ordered by a mix of distance and rating.
Filter results by category and 'open now', and page through them.
Show a place's details: name, address, hours, photos and rating.
Business owners can create a listing and update its details; changes appear in search within 10 minutes.
nonFunctional: Search p99 under 150 ms at the API, excluding the client network.
Handle ~17 k searches/s at peak, mostly reads; writes are ~1 per second.
Results may be up to 10 minutes stale (eventual consistency is fine for listings).
99.9% availability for search; search keeps working if the business database is down.

assumptions: 100 M daily active users, 5 searches each per day
~100 k listing edits and new places per day
A business record is ~1 KB; a geo index entry is ~32 B (id, lat, lng, cell key)

steps.label: Business data size
steps.result: ≈ 200 GB: one Postgres primary with replicas

steps.label: Geo index size
steps.result: ≈ 6–7 GB: fits in RAM on one server

steps.label: Query servers needed
steps.math: assume ~4 k searches/s per server (CPU spent filtering and ranking); 17 k / 4 k ≈ 4.3
steps.result: ≈ 5 servers at peak, ~3 per region × 3 regions for headroom and failover

estimates.takeaway: This is a read-heavy problem with a small index. The whole geo index fits in memory on one box, so we do not need to shard it for size; we replicate it for throughput and availability. Writes are about one per second, so the index can be updated asynchronously and does not need to be fast to write. The interesting work is in the index structure and query planning, not in raw scale.

api.returns: 200 { results: [{ id, name, lat, lng, distanceM, rating }], nextCursor }
api.note: Radius capped at 20 km. The cursor encodes the last (score, id) so the next page continues from there.

api.returns: 200 { id, name, address, hours, photos[], rating, reviewCount }
api.note: Served from a cache in front of the business DB; detail pages are the most cacheable reads.

api.body: { name, lat, lng, address, category, hours }
api.note: Owner-only. Coordinates are geocoded and validated against the address.
Changes to location or category are pushed to the geo index through change data capture.

entities.name: Place
entities.why: Source of truth. 200 GB and ~1 write/s is comfortable for one primary; replicas serve detail reads.

entities.name: GeoIndexEntry
entities.store: In-memory index on each search server
entities.why: A sorted array by cellKey turns 'all places in these cells' into a few binary searches and contiguous scans.

data.note: The database is the source of truth; the geo index is a derived, read-only copy loaded into memory on every search server. Geohash strings sort so that places in the same cell are adjacent, which is why a plain B-tree on geohash already supports WHERE geohash LIKE 'wydm6%'. Storing the hash as a 64-bit integer makes the in-memory version compact and fast. Detail pages read Place by primary key through a cache.

hld.summary:
A search service fleet holds the full geo index in memory. Each query turns the location and radius into a set of cells, scans those cells, filters by exact distance and category, ranks the survivors and returns a page. Search servers do not talk to the database at query time, so the database can be down and search still works.

The business service handles owner edits and writes to Postgres. A change data capture stream carries changes to an index builder, which applies them to the search servers every minute and writes a full snapshot nightly to object storage, so a new server can boot from the snapshot and catch up from the stream. A cache sits in front of detail reads and popular search cells.

diagram.title: Search path and listing update path
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  U[User app] --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> S[Search service with in-memory index]
  LB --> D[Place details service]
  D --> C[(Cache)]
  D --> RR[(Postgres replicas)]
  O[Owner app] --> B[Business service]
  B --> PG[(Postgres primary)]
  PG --> RR
  PG --> CDC[[Change stream]]
  CDC --> IB[Index builder]
  IB --> S
  IB --> SNAP[(Index snapshots)]

flows.title: Searching for coffee within 500 m
steps: The app sends lat, lng, radius 500 m and category coffee.
The search server picks geohash precision 6 (cells about 1.2 km × 0.6 km at the equator) and computes the user's cell plus its 8 neighbours.
It scans the 9 cell ranges in the sorted index, keeping only coffee places.
It computes exact distance for each candidate and drops those beyond 500 m.
It ranks by a blend of distance and rating and returns the first 20 with a cursor.

flows.title: An owner moves their shop
steps: Owner PATCHes new coordinates; the business service writes Postgres.
The change stream emits the update with old and new geohash.
The index builder batches changes for up to 60 s and sends them to every search server.
Each server removes the old entry and inserts the new one; within a few minutes searches show the new location.

flows.title: A new search server starts
steps: It downloads last night's snapshot (~6 GB) from object storage.
It replays the change stream from the snapshot's position.
It reports healthy only when caught up, then the load balancer sends it traffic.

deepDives.title: Choosing the geo index: geohash, quadtree or an R-tree
deepDives.problem: A normal index on latitude and longitude separately cannot answer 'everything within 2 km' efficiently: an index on lat finds a whole horizontal band around the world, and then we filter by lng. We need an index that keeps points that are close on the map close in the index. Density is very uneven: thousands of places per km² in a city centre and one per 100 km² in the countryside.

options.name: Geohash
options.how: Interleave the bits of lat and lng into one key and encode it in base32. Each extra character divides the cell into 32 smaller ones. Places in the same cell share a prefix, so a sorted index on the key turns a cell into a range scan.
pros: Works in any database with a B-tree, or as a sorted array in memory
Easy to shard and cache by prefix
Cheap updates: change one key
cons: Fixed cell sizes: a cell is either too big downtown or too small in the countryside
Cell shapes stretch with latitude
Nearby points across a cell edge can have very different keys

options.name: Quadtree
options.how: Start with the whole world as one node. Split any node holding more than ~100 places into four children, recursively. A search walks down to the leaves that overlap the circle.
pros: Adapts to density: tiny leaves downtown, huge leaves in empty areas
Each leaf holds a predictable number of places, so query cost is steady
cons: Lives in memory as a custom structure; not a database index
Rebuild on startup takes minutes for 200 M places
Harder to shard across machines than flat keys

options.name: R-tree via PostGIS
options.how: Store a geography column and a GiST (R-tree) index; query with a distance function.
pros: No custom code; exact distance queries built in
Good enough up to a few thousand queries per second per replica
cons: Every search hits the database, so read scaling means many replicas
Harder to tune than an in-memory structure at 17 k/s

deepDives.choice: For these numbers I would use geohash keys in an in-memory sorted array on each search server. The index is small (6.4 GB), updates are rare, and geohash gives cheap range scans plus a simple way to cache and shard by prefix later. I would choose a quadtree instead if result counts per query must be predictable everywhere, because its leaves adapt to density. For a first version or a single city, PostGIS on read replicas is the fastest path and is perfectly fine below a few thousand searches per second.

deepDives.title: Geohash precision and edge cases
deepDives.problem: Picking the wrong precision either misses results or scans far too many. At the equator a 6-character cell is about 1.22 km wide and 0.61 km tall; a 5-character cell is about 4.9 km × 4.9 km; a 4-character cell is about 39 km × 19.5 km. Searching the user's cell plus its 8 neighbours only guarantees coverage up to the smaller side of one cell in every direction, because the user may sit at the edge of their cell. There are also edges where geohash behaves badly.

options.name: One precision, 3 × 3 cells
options.how: Pick the finest precision whose smaller cell side is at least the radius, then scan the cell and its 8 neighbours.
pros: Simple: always 9 ranges
Correct as long as the precision rule is followed
cons: Wasteful for large radii: a 5 km radius needs precision 4, so 9 × 39.1 × 19.5 ≈ 6 860 km² scanned to cover a 79 km² circle
Precision 6 cannot be used for 1 km: its 0.61 km height is too small

options.name: Cover the circle with many smaller cells
options.how: Compute the set of cells at a finer precision that overlap the circle's bounding box and merge adjacent keys into ranges.
pros: Scans close to the real circle area
Works for any radius
cons: More ranges per query (tens instead of 9)
More complex query planning code

options.name: Expanding search
options.how: Start at a fine precision; if fewer than N results are found, move one level coarser and repeat.
pros: Returns useful results in sparse areas without a huge default radius
cons: Several round trips in sparse areas
Must deduplicate places seen at the previous level

deepDives.choice: Use a covering of finer cells for large radii and the simple 3 × 3 rule for small ones; add expanding search when a query returns fewer than 10 results. For a 1 km radius, a covering at precision 6 needs at most about 3 × 5 = 15 cells over the 2 km × 2 km box (2 / 1.22 ≈ 1.6, so up to 3 columns once the box straddles cell edges; 2 / 0.61 ≈ 3.3, so up to 5 rows). That is about 15 × 0.74 ≈ 11 km² scanned, against 9 × 24 ≈ 215 km² for the 3 × 3 rule at precision 5. Always confirm candidates with an exact distance check. Edge cases to name out loud: boundaries (two cafés 10 m apart on either side of the equator or the prime meridian share no prefix at all, so neighbour lookup is mandatory, never prefix-only); latitude (at 60° north cells are half as wide east to west, so compute neighbours with a library instead of assuming square cells); the antimeridian and poles (neighbours wrap from +180° to −180°; few places are there, but the code must not crash). If these edges became a constant source of bugs, I would switch to a cell system with uniform neighbours, such as S2 or H3.

diagram.title: Planning one search query
diagram.src:
flowchart TD
  A[Location and radius] --> B{Radius at most 600 m}
  B -->|yes| C[Precision 6 cell plus 8 neighbours]
  B -->|no| D[Cover bounding box with finer cells]
  C --> E[Scan cell ranges in sorted index]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Exact distance and category filter]
  F --> G{At least 10 results}
  G -->|yes| H[Rank and return page]
  G -->|no| I[Widen radius one level]
  I --> D

deepDives.title: Scaling reads to 17 k searches per second
deepDives.problem: Each search reads a few hundred to a few thousand candidates, filters and ranks them. That is CPU work, not storage work. Traffic is also uneven: big cities at lunchtime get far more searches than everywhere else, and many users in the same area ask nearly the same question.

options.name: Replicate the full index to every search server
options.how: Every server holds all 6.4 GB and can answer any query; the load balancer spreads traffic.
pros: No routing logic
Any server can fail without losing coverage
cons: Every server pays memory for the whole world
Each update must reach every server

options.name: Shard the index by region
options.how: Split by geohash prefix or country; a router sends each query to the shard owning its cells.
pros: Less memory per server
Hot cities can get dedicated capacity
cons: Queries near a shard border must hit two shards
Uneven shard sizes because cities are dense

options.name: Cache results per cell and filter
options.how: Cache the ranked candidate list for (precision-6 cell, category) for 5 minutes; nearby users with the same filters hit the cache.
pros: Very high hit rate in dense areas
Cuts CPU for repeated questions
cons: Results are only as precise as the cell; still need an exact distance re-check
Stale for up to the cache TTL

deepDives.choice: Full replication plus a cell-level result cache. At 6.4 GB per copy, every server can hold the world, and about 5 servers handle peak load; I would run 3 per region in 3 regions for failover. The cache keyed by (cell, category) absorbs lunchtime spikes in dense cities. I would only shard by region if the index grew past what one server's memory can comfortably hold (around 50–100 GB, for example after adding rich filters per place) or if regional data residency required it.

deepDives.title: Keeping the index fresh as businesses change
deepDives.problem: Owners change hours, names and occasionally their location. New places open every day. The index is a copy, so it can drift from the database. We need changes to appear within 10 minutes, without rebuilding 200 M entries for each edit and without making owner writes depend on search servers being up.

options.name: Nightly full rebuild only
options.how: Rebuild the index from the database once a day and swap it in.
pros: Very simple
No drift accumulates
cons: Edits take up to a day to show
A failed rebuild leaves the whole index a day older

options.name: Dual write from the business service
options.how: On each edit, write Postgres and then call every search server.
pros: Changes appear in seconds
cons: If a call fails, that server drifts forever
Owner writes slow down or fail when search is unhealthy

options.name: Change data capture plus periodic snapshot
options.how: Stream committed DB changes to an index builder that applies them in small batches; also write a nightly snapshot so new servers start from a recent base.
pros: Changes appear within a minute or two
The DB commit is the only source of truth; no lost updates
Owner writes never depend on search
cons: Needs a CDC pipeline and offset tracking
Must handle out-of-order and duplicate events (use version numbers)

deepDives.choice: CDC plus a nightly snapshot. At about one change per second, batching every 60 s means each server applies ~60 tiny updates a minute. Each event carries the row's version so applying it twice is harmless. The nightly snapshot also fixes any slow drift. If listings needed to show changes instantly for the owner, I would read the owner's own listing from the database on their dashboard rather than make search synchronous.

failures: A search server restarts and its index is empty
It loads the nightly snapshot from object storage, replays the change stream, and reports healthy only when caught up; the load balancer skips it until then.
Search keeps working from the in-memory index. Detail pages are served from cache; owner edits fail with a clear retry message.
The CDC pipeline stalls for hours
Search serves slightly stale data. Alert on stream lag above 10 minutes; the nightly snapshot resets any drift once the pipeline recovers.
A lunchtime spike in one city overloads search CPU
The per-cell result cache absorbs repeated queries; autoscale search servers on CPU; shed expensive queries (very large radius) first.
Bad coordinates put a shop in the ocean
Validate on write by geocoding the address and comparing; flag places whose coordinates are far from their stated city.
scale: 10× searches: 170 k / 4 k ≈ 43, so about 45 servers. Still fully replicated; add more per region and lean harder on the cell cache.
10× places (2 B): index ~64 GB. Still fits on a large server, but boot time and memory cost suggest sharding by geohash prefix with a router.
Richer ranking: personalised ranking needs more candidates per query; move ranking to a second stage that re-scores the top ~200 geo candidates.
Moving objects: if we add live delivery couriers, they get a separate write-optimised index (see ride-hailing) instead of sharing this one.

followups.q: Why not just index latitude and longitude in a normal database?
answer: Two separate B-tree indexes each find a whole band of the planet; the database then intersects or filters huge sets.
A composite (lat, lng) index only helps the first column, so a 'narrow lat band' scan still touches every longitude in that band.
Geohash, quadtrees and R-trees exist to keep nearby points near each other in one index.

followups.q: How would you return the 20 nearest places regardless of radius?
answer: Start with a small set of cells and widen until at least 20 candidates are found, then sort by exact distance.
A quadtree makes this natural: visit leaves in order of distance until 20 are confirmed.
Cap the maximum radius so an empty area does not scan a continent.

followups.q: How do you handle 'open now' across time zones?
answer: Store hours in the place's local time plus its time zone.
At query time convert 'now' to each candidate's time zone; most candidates in one query share a zone, so cache that conversion.
Precompute an 'open in the next hour' bit every few minutes for the most common filter.

followups.q: How does pagination stay stable when places change?
answer: The cursor encodes the last returned (score, id) plus the query parameters.
The next page continues strictly after that score; a place that moved might appear twice or be skipped, which is acceptable for this product.
Never use offset paging on top of a ranked geo query, because results shift between pages.

mistakes: Searching only the user's own geohash cell and missing places just across the edge.
Choosing a geohash precision where the cell is smaller than the radius, so the 3 × 3 neighbours cannot cover it.
Sharding the index for size when 6 GB fits in memory on one server.
Writing to the index synchronously on every business edit, coupling owner writes to search health.
Forgetting the exact distance check after the cell scan, returning places outside the radius.
